messages.subject: Help regarding INLA theories
parts:
Dear INLA experts,

I'm facing some questions while reading through INLA literatures:

1. What does it mean by having the non-linear functions f(.) in the linear predictor as latent variables? How do I interpret these functions in a gaussian context?

2. There seems to be examples of non-gaussian posterior marginals for the latent variables (e.g. Fig 4d, 5a in Rue et al. 2009), but so far I haven't encountered these myself. May I ask what would be the conditions leading to non-gaussian marginals?

Many thanks!

Sincerely,
Louis

On Mon, 2025-02-10 at 20:09 -0800, Louis Li wrote:
> Dear INLA experts,
>
> I'm facing some questions while reading through INLA literatures:
>
> 1. What does it mean by having the non-linear functions f(.) in the linear
> predictor as latent variables? How do I interpret these functions in a
> gaussian context?
the might look non-linear, but they are still linear in the random variables.

>
> 2. There seems to be examples of non-gaussian posterior marginals for the
> latent variables (e.g. Fig 4d, 5a in Rue et al. 2009), but so far I haven't
> encountered these myself. May I ask what would be the conditions leading to
> non-gaussian marginals?

the posterior marginals of the latent is usually pretty symmetric and Gaussian
like, with the exception of 'fixed effects and short random effects that could
be a little skewed.

By default, the skewness of these marginals only come from integration over the
hyperparamters, as the approximation for fixed hyperpameters are Gaussian. THere
is a thesis discussing how to correct this, and work in on the way to make a
such approximation into R-INLA

https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6867-2530
